objetivo.en: Say which part of your body hurts and book a doctor's appointment by phone.

nota.en: Stem change o → ue: duele, duelen.
The stress falls on the second syllable: “es-TOH-mah-goh”.
For a pain inside the ear, Spanish says el oído. The outer ear is la oreja.
Feminine even though it ends in -o: la mano, las manos.

explicacion.en: Doler works like gustar: the body part is the thing that hurts and me says who feels it. Say me duele la cabeza, not “my head hurts”.
The verb agrees with the body part, not with me. One part: duele. Several parts: duelen.
With body parts Spanish uses the article (la, el, los, las), not mi or tu. The pronoun me already tells whose back it is.

texto.en: In English the person owns the pain: “my head hurts”. In Spanish the body part is the thing that hurts, and a pronoun says who feels it: me duele la cabeza. Doler works exactly like gustar. The pronouns are me (I), te (you, informal), le (you, formal; he; she), nos (we) and les (you all; they). The verb agrees with the body part: one part takes duele (me duele la cabeza), several take duelen (me duelen los ojos). Doler changes its stem from o to ue, so you hear duele and duelen: “DWEH-leh”, “DWEH-len”. The body part takes an article (el, la, los, las), never mi or tu: me duele la espalda. To say who, you can add a before the name: a Daniela le duele la cabeza. The doctor asks ¿Qué le duele? (formal); a friend asks ¿Qué te duele? To book an appointment politely, use ¿Podría darme una cita? (“Could you give me an appointment?”).

titulo.en: I have a fever and I feel dizzy

objetivo.en: Describe symptoms to the doctor with tener and estar: tengo fiebre, tengo tos; estoy resfriada, estoy mareada.

nota.en: The same word works as an adjective: estoy resfriada = I have a cold.
Always plural in Spanish: tengo náuseas. Say it “NOW-seh-ahs”.
What a doctor asks a patient. With a friend: ¿qué te pasa?

explicacion.en: Symptoms you have use tener, not estar: tengo fiebre, tengo tos, tengo náuseas. Estar goes with an adjective: estoy mareada.
A temporary state of your body or health takes estar, not ser: estoy resfriada, estoy cansada.
When a woman speaks, the adjective ends in -a: estoy mareada. A man says estoy mareado.

titulo.en: Tener for symptoms, estar for states

texto.en: To tell a doctor what is wrong, Spanish uses two verbs. Use tener for a symptom you have, and usually skip the article: tengo fiebre, tengo tos, tengo náuseas (the exception is tengo un resfriado). Use estar with an adjective that describes your state: estoy mareada, estoy resfriada, estoy cansada. Never use ser for these temporary states. The adjective agrees with the person speaking: Emma, a woman, says estoy mareada; a man says estoy mareado. To say how long you have felt this way, use desde hace + a length of time (tengo tos desde hace dos días) or desde + a starting point (tengo tos desde el lunes). You already know me duele and me duelen from the last class: they work together with these verbs. The doctor starts with ¿Qué le pasa? (“What's wrong?”) and talks to Emma with usted.

objetivo.en: Give a friend advice with deberías + infinitive and understand the pharmacist's advice when buying medicine.

nota.en: The ll sounds like the y in “yes”.
The j is a strong h: “hah-RAH-beh”.
Also used as a noun: comer picante = to eat spicy food.
Softer than debes (“you must”): friendly advice.
The same form also means “I should”, “he should” and “she should”. The context tells you who.

explicacion.en: Deber is followed directly by the infinitive. English “to” does not turn into a: deberías descansar.
For a friend (tú) the form ends in -s: deberías. Debería without the -s is for usted, él or ella.
The negative goes before the verb, not before the infinitive: no deberías comer picante.

texto.en: To give advice Spanish uses deberías + infinitive: deberías descansar (“you should rest”). It is the polite, softer form of deber, the same family as podría and me gustaría. With a friend (tú) say deberías; with one person you address as usted say debería; with several people say deberían. For “we should” use deberíamos. The infinitive follows directly, with no a and no de: deberías beber agua. To say what NOT to do, put no before deber: no deberías comer picante. You also hear commands from the pharmacist with usted: tome una pastilla cada ocho horas (“take one pill every eight hours”). The usted command of tomar is tome, and for ustedes it is tomen.

titulo.en: It is important to drink water

objetivo.en: Give and understand health recommendations with es importante, es mejor and es necesario + infinitive.

nota.en: What a doctor orders: tres días de reposo.

explicacion.en: English “to” does not become a here. Es importante is followed directly by the infinitive: es importante beber agua.
After es importante, es mejor and es necesario use the infinitive, never the -ing form.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Es necesario dormir por ocho horas.

explicacion.en: Spanish does not need por for “for eight hours”: just dormir ocho horas.

texto.en: Last class you gave advice to a person with deberías. Now you give a general recommendation that does not point at anyone: es importante beber agua (“it is important to drink water”). Use es importante, es necesario (the strongest) or es mejor, and put the infinitive right after. The expression does not point at anyone, so it never changes: it is the same for you, for me and for everyone. Do not conjugate the second verb, and do not add a or de: es necesario dormir ocho horas. To say what not to do, put no before the infinitive: es mejor no comer picante. When you list several things you avoid, use ni after a negative idea: es mejor no comer picante ni frituras. A doctor often uses this form because it sounds objective and professional. Compare: deberías descansar (advice to you) and es importante descansar (a general recommendation). You will also hear se for people in general: con un resfriado, se toma una infusión de manzanilla.

titulo.en: I have been training for two months

objetivo.en: Say how long you have been doing a habit or having a symptom: llevo tres días tosiendo, llevo un mes entrenando.

nota.en: The g sounds like a strong h: “heem-NAH-see-oh”.

traduccion.en: to have been (doing something for a time)

nota.en: Llevar also means to carry and to wear. With a time and a gerund it says how long.

explicacion.en: To say how long you have been doing something, use llevar + time + gerund. Estar + gerund only says what is happening right now.
English “I have been training for two months” becomes llevo, not tengo: llevo dos meses entrenando.
After the time expression llevar needs a gerund (-ando or -iendo), not the infinitive.

texto.en: To say how long you have been doing something that started in the past and still goes on, Spanish uses llevar + a length of time + a gerund: llevo dos meses entrenando (“I have been training for two months”). The verb stays in the present: llevo, llevas, lleva, llevamos, llevan. The gerund never changes. Form it by replacing the ending: -ar becomes -ando (caminar → caminando) and -er or -ir become -iendo (correr → corriendo, toser → tosiendo). Dormir is irregular: durmiendo. Compare the two uses of the gerund: estar + gerund is what is happening now (Daniela está corriendo ahora) and llevar + time + gerund is for how long (Daniela lleva un año corriendo). To ask, say ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas entrenando? You can also use the same pattern for symptoms: llevo tres días tosiendo. And you can put the gerund first: llevo entrenando dos meses.
